\chapter{Introduction}
Configuration scripts for cloud infrastructure are notoriously prone to
drift: a value that was correct at first deploy silently becomes wrong
as the surrounding fleet evolves. Operators usually discover the drift
only when an outage traces back to a stale parameter.

This thesis presents a static analyser that flags suspicious parameter
combinations before deployment. The analyser parses the script into a
fact base, applies a rule engine over the facts, and reports violations
ranked by severity. The design goal is zero-configuration adoption: a
team should be able to point the tool at an existing repository and get
useful findings within the first run.

The contributions are threefold. First, a parsing layer that tolerates
the templating constructs found in real-world scripts. Second, a rule
engine whose rules are written as queries over the fact base rather
than as imperative checks. Third, an evaluation on forty open-source
repositories showing that the analyser finds an average of eleven
actionable violations per repository with a false-positive rate below
nine percent.

\chapter{Method}
\section{Fact extraction}
The parser lowers each script into a relational fact base. Statements
become facts keyed by scope, and templating constructs are expanded at
parse time so that downstream rules never see template syntax. Scopes
form a tree that mirrors the directory layout of the repository.

\section{Rule engine}
Rules are datalog-style queries over the fact base. A rule names the
fact patterns that constitute a violation and attaches a severity and
an explanation template. Because rules are declarative, users can write
project-specific rules without touching the analyser itself, and the
engine can evaluate them in any order it finds efficient.

\section{Prototype}
The prototype implements the analyser as a command-line tool over a
SQLite fact base, and the full rule set ships as a separate text file
that the tool loads at startup. Planned extensions of the prototype are
sketched in Section~\ref{sec:future}.

\section{Evaluation}
We ran the prototype on forty open-source repositories selected from
two package registries. Each finding was manually adjudicated by two
of the authors, and disagreements were resolved in a joint session.
The evaluation chapter reports precision, recall against a hand-built
ground truth, and the distribution of severities across repositories.

\chapter{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
We presented a static analyser for configuration scripts that combines
a tolerant parsing layer with a declarative rule engine. On forty
real-world repositories it finds an average of eleven actionable
violations per repository at a false-positive rate below nine percent,
which is competitive with commercial offerings while remaining fully
open source.

\section{Limitations}
The analyser reasons about one repository at a time, so violations that
span several repositories are invisible to it. Dynamic dispatch through
remote templates is also out of scope: the parser expands only the
templating constructs it can resolve statically, and silently skips the
rest.

\section{Future Work}
\label{sec:future}
Three directions remain open. First, the rule engine should learn
templates from example violations instead of shipping a fixed rule set.
Second, a browser plug-in that suggests refactorings directly in the
editor would shorten the feedback loop. Third, the evaluation should be
extended to multi-repository setups where drift crosses project
boundaries.
